issues.item: Triggers: Children Present: Being around children
issues.explanation: For an adult male sexual assault survivor, 'being around children' is not impossible as a trigger, but in this profile it is hard to connect clinically to the rest of the selected items and formulation. The other triggers (related news, motorcycle noise) plausibly cue intrusive memory reactivation, and the memory items are all intrusion/emotion based. 'Being around children' implies a distinct trauma meaning or developmental context that is not reflected anywhere in Memory, Threat, Negative Appraisals, or Maladaptive Strategies. Given the formulation is dominated by Triggers ↔ Memory links, this trigger stands out as insufficiently supported by the accompanying memory content and is the one item most likely to be incoherent.

vignette:
Keanu traces the calluses on his palms, a roofer's hands, but they feel like they belong to a stranger. At forty-eight, he had always believed he understood his own body-its limits, its strengths, its reliable capacity for a hard day's work. That certainty vanished six months ago. The assault happened after a job ran late, a rare weeknight drink with his crew at a dive bar he'd never been to before. He remembers the low growl of a motorcycle pulling into the gravel lot, the man who followed him out to his truck, and the overwhelming, sour smell of cheap whiskey. The details of the attack itself arrive not as a linear story but as brutal, sensory fragments that feel more present and solid than the therapy office chair he now sits in. These memories have a terrible, high-definition quality that makes the rest of his life seem faded and unreal.

In the weeks that followed, the world became a minefield of reminders. The sound of a Harley-Davidson revving at a stoplight could send a jolt of ice through his veins, making him drop a tool on the job site. The scent of alcohol, even a beer opened by his wife, Leilani, in their own kitchen, was enough to make him feel sick and trapped. The most difficult trigger, however, was the most unexpected. The man who attacked him was later arrested in connection with several other assaults, and the story was all over the local news. Now, the mere sight of a news van or the opening theme of the evening broadcast tightens his chest, as if the report is not about a past event but a future threat.

Keanu began to change his life in small, then significant, ways. He threw himself into his work, arriving at job sites before dawn and staying until the last light faded, hoping physical exhaustion would silence his mind. It was a strategy of perpetual motion; he was convinced that if he just kept busy, the memories couldn't catch him. At home, he became a tyrant in his own kitchen. In a life that felt utterly chaotic and violated, controlling what he ate became his one domain of order. He weighed his portions, stuck to a rigid diet, and felt a flicker of calm in the strict denial of appetite. The physical demands of his job, once a source of pride, became another source of terror. The sensation of his lungs burning and muscles straining while carrying a heavy bundle of shingles up a ladder felt too much like the memory of struggling against his attacker. He started telling his partner his back was giving out, avoiding the heaviest loads, a lie that has started to fray the trust between them.

Sometimes, the horror comes without a picture. He can be measuring a roofline, the sun warm on his back, and suddenly be engulfed by a cold wave of pure dread, the exact feeling from that night, but with no accompanying image. It's a disembodied terror that leaves him shaking and disoriented. Other times, the memories bring not fear but an overwhelming grief. He'll recall a specific moment-the glint of the streetlights on the motorcycle's chrome fender-and be swamped by a sorrow so profound it almost knocks him off his feet, a mourning for the man he used to be, the one who felt safe in the world.

He finally sought help after an incident at work. A motorcycle backfired on the street below, and the sudden noise sent a memory crashing into him so vividly that he lost his footing on a steep pitch. His partner grabbed his harness just in time. The look on his friend's face-a mixture of fear and confusion-made Keanu realize he could no longer manage this alone. He is here now because the walls he built to keep the trauma out have become a prison, isolating him from his wife, his work, and himself. He is terrified that he is permanently broken, but a small part of him hopes he can learn to live inside his own skin again without being afraid.
